thread:
alex: Heads-up — staging CI perf regressed after the model-onboard merge (checkpoint + tokenizer shim). CI p99 token latency jumped from ~180ms to ~420ms on the same perf suite. Can someone pick this up? :eyes:

maria: Ugh. I saw the alert. My quick grep shows a new commit landed that flipped the encoding shim to the 'compat' path: `onboard: enable-encoding-shim-compat`.

ben: I started a bisect on the perf job. Early results point to the shim flip + a kernel selector tweak happening in the same PR set. Repro locally with small synthetic workload: p99 went 170 -> 390ms.

sam: Do we have profiler traces from CI? I want to see whether it's tokenizer time or runtime kernel choice causing the spike.

ci-bot: perf-ci-staging: build 2026-03-11-1421 failed perf threshold. p50: 45ms -> 48ms, p95: 160ms -> 210ms, p99: 180ms -> 420ms, allocs: +37%. Full logs: https://ci.internal/reports/2026-03-11-1421

onboard-bot: onboard-checkpoints: checkpoint v12 added (tokenizer v2.1) — note: tokenizer config `normalize_unicode` set to `true` by default in this variant.

alex: Thanks. Ben, if your bisect narrowed it down, call out the commit hashes. Also we should pause the canary rollout for that checkpoint if it's in progress.

ben: Bisect nails it to two commits touching different layers: `a1b2c3d` (tokenizer shim flip) and `d4e5f6g` (kernel selector fallback change: prefer generic_matmul for short seqs). When applied together the perf regression is large; each alone is smaller (~+15-20% p99), together it's +130-140%.

maria: That smells like KV cache key divergence. If tokenizer normalization changes byte encoding, KV keys differ and we lose cache hits -> longer token generation paths and more kernel-fallback calls. Can we check KV cache hit-rate traces?

sam: Pulled profiler from the failing CI run. Top lines:```
Trace summary (staging-2026-03-11-1421)
- tokenize.normalize_unicode: time +2.2ms/op
- runtime.kernel_selector: increased calls to generic_matmul
- kv_cache.lookup.misses: +62% vs baseline
- allocator.allocations: +35% (small object churn)
```

alex: So tokenizer change increases per-request CPU, which increases latency and changes sequence padding distribution, so kernel selector triggers the generic kernel more often, and the KV cache misses amplify token count per request. Compound effect.

ben: I ran an experiment: revert tokenizer shim commit `a1b2c3d` and keep kernel selector change — p99 returns to +18% over baseline (still bad but manageable). Revert the kernel selector commit `d4e5f6g` and keep tokenizer shim — p99 ~ +25%. Reverting both returns to baseline.

maria: Action: pause canary and mark the checkpoint as blocked. I'll create a rollback PR for the tokenizer shim and a follow-up to adjust kernel selector heuristics to be more conservative for short sequences.

sam: Suggestion: add a KV-key compatibility layer: normalize tokens before hashing to maintain key continuity across tokenizer variants. That would avoid mass cache invalidation during onboards.

alex: Good idea. Short term: rollback tokenizer shim (PR in flight), pause checkpoint rollout, and add CI gate that runs a quick perf check when tokenizer or kernel selector code is modified. Long term: implement KV-key normalization and add regression tests for onboards.

ci-bot: ci: started job perf-smoke-onboard-guard for PR #4301 (rollback-tokenizer-shim).

ben: I'll shepherd the rollback PR and attach the profiler traces + bisect notes to the PR description.

maria: Filed blocked-checkpoint ticket: INC-2026-238 (checkpoint v12 blocked, reason: perf regression). Adding owners.

alex: Awesome. Keep updates here. If rollback doesn't clear the canary, we escalate to emergency revert of the entire onboard pipeline. :thumbsup:
